rv.q: With “1972,” Stokes and Nelson have crafted a riveting theatrical concert coupling the kindness of strangers with the battle for reproductive freedom...
Stokes’ poignant and inspiring songs (based on the book co-written with Jessie Nelson, director and author of Waitress) are stand-alone knockouts and a coherent libretto.
And this new rock opera by Chadwick Stokes warrants that adjective.

Smith’s writing sings under Tasia A. Jones’ excellent direction, supported by Lindsey McWhorter’s artful choreography, Janie E. Howland’s scenic design and Pamela Hersch’s projections of swaying trees, stained glass and more.
It’s difficult to call a show flawless, but musician-activist Chadwick Stokes’ “1972” delivers something truly special through a blend of live music and deeply emotional storytelling.
The energy and emotional delivery of the two dozen well-written and beautifully performed songs as they flow into one another make the story absorbing and moving.

Nonetheless, at Wednesday’s press night, 1972 proved not only ultimately triumphant in its cry for women’s empowerment but also practically seamless in its crisp, exhilarating interchange of instrumentalists, singers, and actors.
A.R.T.’s rousing production of 1972 will bring you to your feet.
For now, 1972 lets us relish in the joy, and I’m so, so grateful for it.
1972 is currently playing a world premiere engagement at American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts... and it is, at present, a very poor piece of theatre.

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this world-premiere rock opera for its exhilarating live music and emotional storytelling, though some find its handling of darker themes uneven. Most call it uplifting and timely.
